name: Blaufränkisch
say: BLOUW-fren-kish, in Hungary KAYK-frahn-kosh, in Germany LEM-ber-ger

lines.s10: Blaufränkisch is the serious red of Austria's Burgenland: black cherry, blackberry and cracked black pepper on bright acidity and a firm grip.
lines.s20: Blaufränkisch is central Europe's dark, peppery red, at home in Burgenland on Austria's eastern edge. It tastes of black cherry and blackberry with cracked black pepper, and its bright acidity and firm tannin let it age for years.
lines.s45: Blaufränkisch comes from Burgenland, the eastern edge of Austria along the Hungarian border, and it is the country's red with backbone. It tastes of black cherry and blackberry with a note of cracked black pepper, on bright acidity, firm tannin and a medium to full body. The lighter wines are raised in steel or large old casks and the fuller ones in oak barrels, with less new wood than a generation ago. Pour it with roast duck, venison or a goulash rich with paprika. Hungary calls the same grape Kékfrankos and Germany calls it Lemberger, so you may have met it under another name.
lines.sale: Blaufränkisch gives you the pepper of a Syrah with the lift of a cool climate red, its black cherry kept bright by acidity. I would pour it with the duck, or for anyone who finds Cabernet too heavy and Pinot Noir too light.

glass.lead: Black cherry and blackberry with cracked black pepper and a cool edge of iron, on bright acidity and firm tannin.

ladder.where: The Eisenberg, the Leithaberg, and Sopron across the lake in Hungary
Mittelburgenland, on deep clay in its sheltered basin

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, tannin medium plus and firm, alcohol medium, body medium to full.

home.home: Burgenland, on Austria's border with Hungary. Mittelburgenland, on deep clay, gives the darker, broader wines; the Leithaberg, on limestone and schist, and the Eisenberg, on iron rich slate, give tauter, more peppery ones. Across the lake, Sopron in Hungary makes it lighter, as Kékfrankos, and Eger and Szekszárd build their Bikavér blends on it.
home.abroad: Germany grows it as Lemberger in Württemberg, from light and fruity to firm and tannic. Washington State and New York's Finger Lakes bottle it under either name. Slovenia knows it as Modra Frankinja and Slovakia as Frankovka.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius: a touch cooler than a Cabernet.
service.glass: A Burgundy bowl for the perfume and the pepper; a Bordeaux glass for a dark, oaked Reserve.
service.decant: Consider it for a young, firm single vineyard wine, after tasting a sample.
service.age: Five to fifteen years for the serious wines; the lighter ones drink well young.

with.why: bright acidity cuts the fat, pepper meets the skin
black cherry and an iron edge suit game
the dish of its home, paprika meeting pepper
firm tannin takes the char and the fat

labels.means: The Hungarian name: lighter and brighter from Sopron, and the frame of the Bikavér blends of Eger and Szekszárd.
The German name, at home in Württemberg and used in Washington and New York too.
The Burgenland origin that admits this grape alone; the growers call it Blaufränkischland.
Two more Burgenland origins led by the grape: limestone and schist, and iron rich slate.

guest.q: I like Syrah. Is this anything like it?
guest.a: It is a near neighbour. You get the same cracked black pepper and blackberry, but Blaufränkisch is lighter on its feet, with brighter acidity and none of Syrah's smoked meat and black olive.
No, the cheese is Limburger. Lemberger is the German name of this grape, and the likeness is one reason some American growers now print Blaufränkisch on the label.

guest.q: Will it keep, or should we drink it now?
guest.a: Both. A simple bottle is ready on release. A single vineyard wine from Burgenland softens over five to fifteen years and turns towards violet and graphite.

compare.tell: Zweigelt, its offspring, is softer and juicier, with sour cherry and medium tannin; Blaufränkisch is darker, more peppery, higher in acidity and firmer.
Syrah is fuller and meatier, with black olive and smoked meat beside its pepper; Blaufränkisch is leaner, with higher acidity and a sour cherry edge.
Cabernet Franc shows green bell pepper, pencil shavings and raspberry; Blaufränkisch has black pepper in place of green, black cherry and brighter acidity.

cards.front: Blaufränkisch: its name in Hungary, and its name in Germany?
cards.back: Kékfrankos in Hungary, where Sopron is its capital and it frames Egri Bikavér. Lemberger in Germany, grown chiefly in Württemberg.

cards.front: Blaufränkisch: name the three Burgenland origins led by it, with their soils.
cards.back: Mittelburgenland, on deep clay: dark and broad. Leithaberg, on limestone and schist: taut and stony. Eisenberg, on iron rich slate: peppery and firm. Rosalia admits it beside Zweigelt.

cards.front: Blaufränkisch blind: what gives it away, and what is it mistaken for?
cards.back: Black cherry and cracked black pepper on high acidity and firm tannin. Syrah is meatier, with black olive; Zweigelt is softer and juicier.

questions.q: A deep ruby red poured blind shows black cherry, blackberry and a clear note of cracked black pepper, with high acidity, firm tannin and no smoked meat or olive. The taster calls central Europe. Which grape fits?
questions.exp: Pepper, black cherry, high acidity and firm tannin mark Blaufränkisch. Zweigelt, the nearest wrong answer, is softer and juicier, and Syrah would be meatier, with black olive.

questions.q: A guest back from Budapest asks for the grape he drank there as Kékfrankos. The list holds four Austrian reds. Which do you bring?
questions.exp: Kékfrankos is Hungary's name for Blaufränkisch. Zweigelt is its offspring, a crossing with Saint Laurent, and Blauburgunder is Austria's name for Pinot Noir.

questions.q: A guest wants a Blaufränkisch in the dark, ripe, broad style that comes from deep clay in a sheltered basin. Which origin do you look for?
questions.exp: Mittelburgenland's deep clay and sheltered warmth give the darker, broader wines. Eisenberg, on iron rich slate, and the Leithaberg, on limestone and schist, are tauter, and the Neusiedlersee is Zweigelt country.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: the home is Burgenland with Hungary across the lake, and Germany, the United States, Slovenia and Slovakia stand as abroad.

The two Codex records disagree on structure: the reviewed profile and the tasting dials give acidity high and tannin medium to high, the Régionale row gives tannin at its top mark. The entry follows the reviewed profile: acidity high, tannin medium plus and firm.

The tasting dials call the grape cool climate, while the Codex's own Burgenland reading calls Mittelburgenland the warmest Pannonian pocket. The ladder puts the Eisenberg, the Leithaberg and Sopron on the cool rung and Mittelburgenland on the moderate one, which agrees with both.
The profile's baking spice is named as clove, and its forest herbs are left out of the glass for want of a source that names the herb.
Less new wood than a generation ago stands on the Codex's own producer note (made without the heavy oak that marked Austrian reds in the 1990s) and on the trade press.

The Limburger answer stands on two writers of the Finger Lakes who report the confusion and on a grower's page that says it changed its label from one name to the other; no Washington source was found for it, so the answer says American growers and no more.

Left out for want of a second source or of room: the first use of the name at a Vienna exhibition in 1862, Lemberger reaching Germany in 1877, the parentage (Blaue Zimmettraube and Weisser Heunisch, per the German wine institute) and the tradition that Frankish once marked a noble vine.
The respelling BLOUW is meant to rhyme with now; a checker may prefer another spelling of that sound.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the sites directly. The checker should open the four addresses.
